question: The cornea remains transparent despite being a living tissue. Which mechanism is the MOST critical for maintaining corneal dehydration (deturgescence) and hence transparency?

answers.text: The regularly arranged collagen lamellae of the stroma that minimise light scatter

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Regular collagen arrangement reduces scatter but deturgescence (active fluid removal) is the primary transparency mechanism. Oedema disrupts the regular spacing and causes cloudiness.

answers.text: Active Na-K-ATPase pump in the corneal endothelium that removes excess water from the stroma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The endothelial Na-K-ATPase (bicarbonate-dependent) pump actively transports fluid out of the stroma. Loss of endothelial cells below ~500 cells/mm² leads to stromal oedema and bullous keratopathy.

answers.text: The avascular nature of the cornea that prevents inflammatory exudates from entering

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Avascularity prevents inflammatory oedema but does not actively remove water already present. The endothelial pump is the active dehydrating mechanism.

answers.text: Mucin layer of the tear film that seals the corneal surface and prevents evaporative loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The mucin layer stabilises the tear film but acts on the outer surface, not on stromal water content. Stromal deturgescence is an endothelial function.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the concept of corneal deturgescence. The endothelial Na-K-ATPase pump is the primary mechanism — loss leads to bullous keratopathy.
Well done! The endothelial pump is the cornerstone of corneal transparency — this is why endothelial cell count is critical before any intraocular surgery.
